This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Mercury's Craters

![](../bobpics/allplanetsiconmercury.png)

Before 1974, nobody really knew what Mercury looked like. It was known to be small and shaped like a ball (hey, that rhymes!), but that’s about it. Things changed though when Mariner 10 became the first space craft to visit Mercury in 1974. It flew past the planet three times, taking as many photographs as it possibly could each time it went by. You’ll never guess what those photos revealed. Okay, you probably will if you’ve looked at the title of this page. It revealed craters. Lots and lots of craters. If you get excited about craters, you’d love Mercury. If you don’t, well, there’s always Mars. Hang on, that has craters too. What about Jupiter? Yes, you’ll like Jupiter. It’s just gas. Anyway, Jupiter can wait. We’re here to talk about Mercury’s craters. Prepare to be astounded!

![](../../bobpics/mercurycraterswide.png)

---

#### What are Craters and why are they there?

Craters are dents made on a planet’s surface from the impact of rocks as they smash into them. During the formation of the solar system, hundreds of thousands of rocks collided into each other over a period of millions of years. Larger rocks clumped together and became larger and larger until they eventually formed the planets that we know and love today. Even after the planets had formed, there were, and still are, rocks flying around the solar system and colliding with the planets.

  

Mercury has the most craters of all of the planets in the solar system. This is for three reasons:

![](../../bobpics/)

1

Mercury is close to the Sun. As the Sun is gigantically huge, it has a strong pull of gravity which attracts nearby debris. Sometimes though, some of this debris hits poor old Mercury instead, leaving an impact on its surface.

2

Mercury doesn’t have an atmosphere. An atmosphere is a layer of gas that surrounds a planet. The other inner planets (Venus, Earth and Mars) all have an atmosphere which protects their surfaces. If rocks head for Earth, they usually burn up in its atmosphere. When this happens, they are quite often referred to as shooting stars because they glow as they fly through the sky. Mars’ atmosphere is very thin which is why it also has craters.

3

Mercury has no weather. Weather events like wind and rain help to redesign a planet’ surface appearance. Wind erodes surface details while rain washes them away. Mercury has none of this.

![](../../bobpics/)

---

Late Heavy Bombardment Period

Although the solar system's planets and larger moons formed about 4.6 billion years ago as a result of collisions of rocks which eventually amassed and became the ball-shaped worlds that we know today, it is thought that most of the craters still visible on objects like Mercury, Mars and the Moon aren't as old as the worlds themselves. About 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, the inner planets came under an unusually heavy bombardment of asteroids and rocks. As it was around 600 million years after the objects formed, it is referred to as the Late Heavy Bombardment. It's not known what caused it although most guesses suggest there may have been a disturbance of asteroids in the asteroid belt which sent many of them into the inner solar system.

![](../../bobpics/)

---

Basins

Some of Mercury’s craters are so large that they aren’t even called craters. Instead they are called basins. These are craters that have a width of more than 400 kilometres (250 miles).  
  
 The largest basin on Mercury is the Caloris Planitia basin. It has a diameter of about 1,525 kilometres (948 miles) and is thought to have been created by an object over 100 kilometres (62 miles) wide crashing into the planet around 3.8 billion years ago. The impact was so great that it caused visible ripple and shock waves on the planet. Smashing.  
  
 As the floor of the Caloris Planitia basin is quite smooth, it suggests that it was created after the heavy bombardment phase. This makes it one of Mercury's youngest basins.

![](../../bobpics/mercury_calorisbasin.jpg) 

Caloris basin from MESSENGER spacecraft, image credit:  [NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington](https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/beta/catalog/PIA19213)

---

Naming Craters

Many of the largest craters on Mercury are given names. This helps scientists to know what they looking at and to find their way around the planet. They don’t just pick random names for craters though, like Keith, John, Barbara, Britney. No, craters on Mercury are named after famous people from the arts world – poets, musicians, actors, writers and so on. The only rule is that they must have been famous for over fifty years and have died more than three years before the naming of the crater. There’s a Disney crater on Mercury, named after Walt Disney. There’s also a Lennon crater, named after John Lennon, a famous singer and songwriter in The Beatles. I suppose that means there actually is a crater called John then!  
  
 The actress who played the Good Witch in the film *The Wizard of Oz* (Billie Burke) has her very own crater on Mercury, as well as PL Travers who created *Mary Poppins*. Other famous people with craters named after them include classical composers Bach, Beethoven and Strauss, writers like Ernest Hemingway Charles Dickens, William Shakespeare and JRR Tolkein (writer of *The Hobbit* and *Lord of the Rings*) and artists like Vincent Van Gogh, Rembrandt and Renoir.

![](../../bobpics/)

---

Ice Ice Baby

Hidden inside some of Mercury’s craters is frozen water. Water is probably the last thing you’d expect to find on a planet so close to the Sun. Mercury’s surface can be as hot as 427 °c (801 °F) when it is facing the Sun. However the floors of some craters are in permanent shade from the Sun.  
  
 These craters are located around Mercury’s north and south poles and are deep and have high rims. This means that any ice in them never melts because heat from the Sun can never reach the dark depths of them. How the water got there is another matter, with the most likely reason being that it was carried by a comet or other space rock that crashed into Mercury.

![](../../bobpics/mercury_waterincraters.jpg) 

Water ice in Mercury's north polar regions as observed by MESSENGER, yellow regions highlight areas of water - the water isn't actually yellow. Image credit:  [NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington](https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/beta/catalog/PIA19213)

##### CHOREOGRAPHER

## George Balanchine

St. Petersburg, Russia

### I don’t want people who want to dance. I want people who have to dance.

##### GEORGE BALANCHINE © THE GEORGE BALANCHINE TRUST

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%20210%20140%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

George Balanchine rehearsing Boston Ballet dancers in Scotch Symphony (circa 1963)  
 Photographer unknown

## Biography

Born in St. Petersburg, Russia, George Balanchine (1904–1983) is regarded as the foremost contemporary choreographer in the world of ballet. He came to the United States in late 1933 at the age of 29, accepting the invitation of the young American arts pa­tron Lincoln Kirstein (1907–96), whose great passions included the dream of creating a ballet company in America. At Balanchine’s behest, Kirstein was also prepared to support the formation of an American academy of ballet that would eventually rival the long-established schools of Europe.

This was the School of American Ballet, found­ed in 1934, the first product of the Balanchine–Kirstein collaboration. Several ballet companies directed by the two were created and dissolved in the years that followed, while Balanchine found other outlets for his choreography. Eventually, with a performance on October 11, 1948, the New York City Ballet was born. Balanchine served as its ballet master and principal choreographer from 1948 until his death in 1983.

Balanchine’s more than 400 dance works include *Serenade* (1934); *Concerto Barocco* (1941); *Le Palais de Cristal*, later renamed *Symphony in C* (1947); *Or­pheus* (1948); *The Nutcracker* (1954); *Agon* (1957); *Symphony in Three Movements* (1972); *Stravinsky Violin Concerto* (1972); *Vienna Waltzes* (1977); *Bal­lo della Regina* (1978); and *Mozartiana* (1981). His final ballet, a new version of Stravinsky’s *Variations for Orchestra*, was created in 1982.

He also choreographed for films, operas, revues and musicals. Among his best-known dances for the stage is *Slaughter on Tenth Avenue*, originally created for Broadway’s *On Your Toes* (1936). The musical was later made into a movie.

A major artistic figure of the 20th century, Bal­anchine revolutionized the look of classical ballet. Taking classicism as his base, he heightened, quick­ened, expanded, streamlined and even inverted the fundamentals of the 400-year-old language of aca­demic dance. This had an inestimable influence on the growth of dance in America. Although at first his style seemed particularly suited to the energy and speed of American dancers, especially those he trained, his ballets are now performed by all the ma­jor classical ballet companies throughout the world.

## 10 Things You Should Know

**1.** Affectionately known as “Mr. B.”  
 **2.** Was Artistic Director of New York City Ballet for 35 years. He co-founded New York City Ballet in 1948 with Lincoln Kirstein and served as the ballet master and principal choreographer until his death.  
 **3.** Made his on-stage debut when he was just ten. Balanchine appeared as the cupid in the Mariisnky Theatre Ballet Company production of *The Sleeping Beauty*.  
 **4.** Directed 10 ballets for Boston Ballet between 1963 and 1973. These included *Apollo* (1965), and *Scotch Symphony* (1965). Balanchine also served as Boston Ballet’s artistic advisor for several years.  
 **5.** Has a crater on Mercury named after him. Acquired by NASA on June 29, 2011, the crater radiates blue-colored rays that are similar in hue to the tutus in *Serenade*.  
 **6.** Created an estimated 465 works in his lifetime.  
 **7.** Recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Balanchine was one of five recipients to receive this award in 1983 from President Ronald Reagan, who praised Balanchine for “lifting our spirits and broadening our horizons through his talent and art.”  
 **8.** Credited with inventing the “neoclassical style.” He combined classical technique with explosive movements and energizing turns. His choreography was graceful yet full of speed and athletic prowess, stretching the boundaries of ballet.  
 **9.** Studied piano at the same conservatory as Tchaikovsky. As a pianist and the son of a well-known Georgian composer, Balanchine had a keen understanding of music theory and composition. He believed dance should showcase the music, rather than the other way around. He was often quoted as saying “See the music, hear the dance.”  
 **10.** Choreographed a ballet for 50 elephants. Balanchine was commissioned by the Ringling Bros., Barnum & Bailey Circus to create *Circus Polka* (1942), a ballet that featured 50 elephants and 50 ballerinas dancing to music by Igor Stravinsky.

## Timeline of George Balanchine’s Life

**1904:** Born in St. Petersburg, Russia.  
 **1913:** Begins studies at the Imperial Theater School.  
 **1920:** Choreographs his first piece, a duet entitled *La Nuit*. Enters the St. Petersburg Conservatory of Music.  
 **1925:** Joins Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes in Paris and becomes his principal choreographer. Balanchine also meets Igor Stravinsky, who will become a life-long friend and collaborator.  
 **1933:** Boston-born dance connoisseur Lincoln Kirstein persuades Balanchine to relocate to the United States.  
 **1934:** Kirstein and Balanchine establish the School of American Ballet. Soon after, they set up a touring company of dancers from the school and call it the American Ballet.  
 **1948:** Balanchine co-founds New York City Ballet (NYCB) with Kirstein. Balanchine will serve as NYCB’s ballet master and principal choreographer until his death.  
 **1964:** The Ford Foundation grants almost $8 million to the New York City Ballet. The company moves to its home at Lincoln Center.  
 **1972:** Balanchine stages NYCB’s first festival, an intensive one-week celebration of the music of Igor Stravinsky.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg/250px-Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg)

The [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom")

This is a partial **list of recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom**, listed chronologically within the aspect of life in which each recipient is or was renowned.

The [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") is awarded by the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative".[[1]](#cite_note-1) Before 1970, honorees were either selected by the president or recommended to them by the [Distinguished Civilian Service Awards Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Civilian_Service_Awards_Board "Distinguished Civilian Service Awards Board").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_recipients&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Typically the medal is bestowed upon the recipient by the sitting president who has chosen them. However, the first recipients selected by president [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") before [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") were formally awarded by his successor in office, [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson").[[3]](#cite_note-id26165-3)

President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") awarded 118 medals, the most of any president, followed by President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") with 89 medal recipients.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Three people—[Ellsworth Bunker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellsworth_Bunker "Ellsworth Bunker"), [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell"), and [Ben Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Carson "Ben Carson")—are two-time recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Powell received his second award with distinction, while Bunker was given both of his awards with distinction.[[5]](#cite_note-2ndPMoF-5)

Eight presidents have themselves received the medal posthumously, post-presidency, or prior to being elected:

* [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") (1963, posthumously)
* [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson") (1980, posthumously)
* [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") (1993, with distinction)
* [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") (1999)
* [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") (1999)
* [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") (2011)
* [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") (2013)
* [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (2017, as Vice President; with distinction)

In 2015, Obama stated that there was no precedent to revoke a Presidential Medal of Freedom, regarding the award given to stand-up comedian and actor [Bill Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby "Bill Cosby").[[6]](#cite_note-6) After being awarded the medal in 2002 by Obama's predecessor, [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), Cosby was [convicted of multiple counts of sexual assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby_sexual_assault_cases "Bill Cosby sexual assault cases"), though the convictions were later overturned.[[7]](#cite_note-ctv-overturned-7)

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is related to, but distinct from, the [Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Freedom_(1945) "Medal of Freedom (1945)"), an earlier award issued between 1945 and 1963 to honor US civilian contributions to [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

In 2022 at the age of 25, athlete and activist [Simone Biles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_Biles "Simone Biles") became the youngest person to receive the award.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

### Declinations of the award

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_recipients&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Declinations of the award")]

[Bill Belichick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Belichick "Bill Belichick"), coach of the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots"), was offered the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), and initially accepted it, but changed his mind and turned down the medal after the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Country musician [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton") turned down the medal twice from Donald Trump. Parton said she turned it down the first time because her husband was ill, and the second time because of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[10]](#cite_note-10)

**Alvin Ailey Jr.** (January 5, 1931 – December 1, 1989) was an American dancer, director, [choreographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choreographer "Choreographer"), and activist. He founded the [Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Ailey_American_Dance_Theater "Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater") (AAADT) in 1958, and the [Clark Center for the Performing Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Center_for_the_Performing_Arts "Clark Center for the Performing Arts") in 1959. He created AAADT and its affiliated Alvin Ailey American Dance Center (later Ailey School) as havens for nurturing Black artists and expressing the universality of the African-American experience through dance.

Ailey's work fused theater, modern dance, ballet, and jazz with Black vernacular, creating hope-fueled choreography that is credited with spreading global awareness of Black life in America. His choreographic masterpiece *[Revelations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revelations_(Alvin_Ailey) "Revelations (Alvin Ailey)")* is recognized as one of the most popular and most performed ballets in the world.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

On July 15, 2008, the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") passed a resolution designating AAADT a "vital American cultural ambassador to the World".[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) That same year, in recognition of AAADT's 50th anniversary, then Mayor [Michael Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg") declared December 4 "Alvin Ailey Day" in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), while then-Governor [David Paterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Paterson "David Paterson") honored the organization on behalf of [New York State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State "New York State").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alvin_Ailey&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Ailey was born to Alvin Ailey and Lula Elizabeth Cliff[[7]](#cite_note-:5-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-BHN-9) in [Rogers, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers,_Texas "Rogers, Texas"), in his maternal grandfather's home on January 5, 1931, at the height of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States"). Growing up in the violently racist and segregated south, Ailey was barred from interacting with mainstream society during his youth.[[10]](#cite_note-10) When he was five, Ailey's mother was raped by four white men (one likely an employer), and Ailey recalled seeing members of the [Ku Klux Klan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan") as a child.[[11]](#cite_note-:3-11)[[12]](#cite_note-:4-12)

The elder Alvin Ailey abandoned the young Alvin and Lula shortly after Alvin was born, leaving Lula to work in cotton fields and as a [domestic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_servant "Domestic servant") in white homes — the only employment available to her.[[13]](#cite_note-13) By the time Ailey was five, he joined his mother picking cotton.[[12]](#cite_note-:4-12) After white men raped Lula in 1936, Ailey began to fear white men.[[7]](#cite_note-:5-7) As an escape, Ailey found refuge in the church, sneaking out at night to watch adults dance, and in writing a journal, a practice that he maintained his entire life. Even this could not shield him from a childhood spent moving from town to town as his mother sought employment, being abandoned with relatives whenever she took off on her own.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[9]](#cite_note-BHN-9)

Looking for greater job prospects, Ailey's mother departed for [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") in 1941. He arrived a year later, enrolling at George Washington Carver Junior High School, and then graduating into [Thomas Jefferson High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_High_School_(Los_Angeles,_California) "Jefferson High School (Los Angeles, California)").[[15]](#cite_note-15) Ailey was able to explore the arts in high school, singing in glee club and writing poetry.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) He also took gymnastics.[[11]](#cite_note-:3-11) Ailey frequently attended the [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Theater_(Los_Angeles) "Lincoln Theater (Los Angeles)") and [Orpheum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheum_Theatre_(Los_Angeles) "Orpheum Theatre (Los Angeles)") Theatres, where he was able to see a variety of African American performers, including [Pearl Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Bailey "Pearl Bailey"), [Fletcher Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Henderson "Fletcher Henderson"), [Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Holiday "Billie Holiday"), [Lena Horne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Horne "Lena Horne"), [Pigmeat Markham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigmeat_Markham "Pigmeat Markham"), [Count Basie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Basie "Count Basie"), and [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington").[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) In 1946, Ailey had his first experience with concert dance when he saw [Ballet Russe de Monte-Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet_Russe_de_Monte-Carlo "Ballet Russe de Monte-Carlo") on a school trip and [Katherine Dunham Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katherine_Dunham_Company "Katherine Dunham Company")'s "Tropical Review" on solitary trips to the Los Angeles Philharmonic Auditorium.[[17]](#cite_note-17) This awakened an until then unknown spark of joy within Ailey.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Also in high school, Ailey discovered his homosexuality, which added another layer of difference and isolation to his already racially segregated experience. Thus, "like many young gay men eager to corral the sensual impulses of the body, he turned to dance study."[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) Ailey briefly studied tap, followed by exploring "primitive dance", as taught by Dunham dancer [Thelma Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelma_Robinson "Thelma Robinson"). Neither of these styles were right for Ailey, possibly due to the physical location and old-fashioned sensibility of the lessons.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) Therefore, he did not become serious about dance until 1949 when his classmate and friend [Carmen De Lavallade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_De_Lavallade "Carmen De Lavallade") dragged Ailey to the [Melrose Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melrose_Avenue "Melrose Avenue") studio of [Lester Horton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Horton "Lester Horton") and he began exploring modern dance.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Ailey studied a wide range of dance styles and techniques — from ballet to Native American inspired movement studies — at Horton's school, which was one of the first racially integrated dance schools in the United States.[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22) Though Horton became his mentor,[[23]](#cite_note-23) Ailey did not commit to dancing full-time, recognizing the lack of opportunities for black male dancers.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) Instead, he pursued academic courses, studying [romance languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_language "Romance language") and writing at [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") (1949),[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-Dunning-25) [Los Angeles City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_College "Los Angeles City College") (1950–1951), and [San Francisco State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_State_University "San Francisco State University") (1952). During this time, Ailey sporadically returned to Horton to work between courses.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) Living in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), he met [Maya Angelou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Angelou "Maya Angelou"), then known as Marguerite Johnson,[[26]](#cite_note-Shepeard-26) with whom Ailey formed a nightclub act called "Al and Rita".[[27]](#cite_note-27) Eventually, he returned to study dance with Horton in Los Angeles.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alvin_Ailey&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Horton Dance Company

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alvin_Ailey&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Horton Dance Company")]

Ailey joined Horton's dance company in 1953. While there, he took daily technique classes, studied art and music, and taught children's classes. That same year, he made his debut in Horton's *Revue Le Bal Caribe*. In a workshop the summer of 1953, Ailey created his first dance composition, *Afternoon Blues*. This work was a three-minute solo blues adaptation of *[L'Aprés-midi d'un Faune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afternoon_of_a_Faun_(Nijinsky) "Afternoon of a Faun (Nijinsky)")*, which he had seen performed by the Ballet Russe de Monte-Carlo. In this piece, Ailey played the eponymous Faun to a selection from *[On the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Town_(musical) "On the Town (musical)")*.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16)

Horton died suddenly November 1953 from a heart attack, leaving the company without leadership.[[29]](#cite_note-29) In order to complete the organization's pressing professional engagements, and because nobody else was willing to, Ailey took over as artistic director and choreographer.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31) In particular, Horton's company was committed to performing at [Jacob's Pillow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob's_Pillow_Dance "Jacob's Pillow Dance") in the summer of 1954. Ailey worked collaboratively with the Horton company dancers and choreographed based on them, gaining the support of the company's dancers who had much more experience than Ailey. These works included *According to St. Francis* (4 June 1954), a tribute to Horton as a "kind of allusion to Lester's life" featuring James Truitte. He also choreographed and directed *Morning Mourning* (4 June 1954)*,* a piece based on[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) the work of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams") featuring de Lavallade and set to an original score by [Gertrude Rivers Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_Rivers_Robinson "Gertrude Rivers Robinson").[[16]](#cite_note-:0-16) As Horton had done, Ailey designed the sets for *Morning Mourning* and collaborated on the lighting. That summer, Ailey also made his first large group piece, *Creation of the World* (13 July 1954), set to a score by [Darius Milhaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_Milhaud "Darius Milhaud"). Under Ailey, the Horton company had commercial engagements on television programs *Party at Ciro's*, [The Red Skelton Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Red_Skelton_Show "The Red Skelton Show"), and the [Jack Benny show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Benny_show "Jack Benny show"). **Edward Kennedy** "**Duke**" **Ellington** (April 29, 1899 – May 24, 1974) was an American [jazz pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_piano "Jazz piano"), composer, and leader of his eponymous [jazz orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") from 1924 through the rest of his life. Music critic [Ralph J. Gleason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_J._Gleason "Ralph J. Gleason") called him "America's most important composer".[[2]](#cite_note-NYTObit-2)

Born and raised in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), Ellington was based in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") from the mid-1920s and gained a national profile through his orchestra's appearances at the [Cotton Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_Club "Cotton Club") in [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"). A master at writing miniatures for the three-minute [78 rpm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph_record#78_rpm_disc_developments "Phonograph record") recording format, Ellington wrote or collaborated on more than one thousand compositions; his extensive body of work is the largest recorded personal jazz legacy, and many of his pieces have become [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). He also recorded songs written by his bandsmen, such as [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol")'s "[Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(Juan_Tizol_and_Duke_Ellington_song) "Caravan (Juan Tizol and Duke Ellington song)")", which brought a [Spanish tinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_tinge "Spanish tinge") to [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") jazz.

At the end of the 1930s, Ellington began a nearly thirty-year collaboration with composer-arranger-pianist [Billy Strayhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Strayhorn "Billy Strayhorn"), whom he called his writing and arranging companion.[[3]](#cite_note-3) With Strayhorn, he composed multiple extended compositions, or suites, as well as many short pieces. For a few years at the beginning of Strayhorn's involvement, Ellington's orchestra featured bassist [Jimmy Blanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Blanton "Jimmy Blanton") and tenor saxophonist [Ben Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Webster "Ben Webster"), and reached what many claim to be a creative peak for the group.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Some years later, following a low-profile period, an appearance by Ellington and his orchestra at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") in July 1956 led to a major revival and regular world tours. Ellington recorded for most American record companies of his era, performed in and scored several films, and composed a handful of stage musicals.

Although a pivotal figure in the [history of jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), in the opinion of [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller") and [Barry Kernfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Kernfeld "Barry Kernfeld"), "the most significant composer of the genre",[[5]](#cite_note-GroveJazz-5) Ellington himself embraced the phrase "beyond category", considering it a liberating principle, and referring to his music as part of the more general category of American music.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Ellington was known for his inventive use of the orchestra, or big band, as well as for his eloquence and charisma. He was awarded a posthumous [Pulitzer Prize Special Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards") for music [in 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Pulitzer_Prize#Other_awards "1999 Pulitzer Prize").[[7]](#cite_note-pulitzer-7)

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Duke_Ellington&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Ellington was born on April 29, 1899, to James Edward Ellington and Daisy (*née*  Kennedy) Ellington in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Both of his parents were pianists. Daisy primarily played [parlor songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlour_music "Parlour music") and James preferred operatic [arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrothers201810-8) They lived with Daisy's parents at 2129 Ida Place (now Ward Place) NW, in D.C.'s [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_(Washington,_D.C.) "West End (Washington, D.C.)") neighborhood.[[9]](#cite_note-Lawrence-1-9) Duke's father was born in [Lincolnton, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincolnton,_North_Carolina "Lincolnton, North Carolina"), on April 15, 1879, and in 1886, moved to D.C. with his parents.[[10]](#cite_note-Lawrence-2-10) Daisy Kennedy was born in Washington, D.C., on January 4, 1879, the daughter of two former [American slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States").[[9]](#cite_note-Lawrence-1-9)[[11]](#cite_note-11) James Ellington made blueprints for the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy").

When Ellington was a child, his family showed racial pride and support in their home, as did many other families. African Americans in D.C. worked to protect their children from the era's [Jim Crow laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws "Jim Crow laws").[[12]](#cite_note-12)

At the age of seven, Ellington began taking piano lessons from Marietta Clinkscales.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrothers201810-8) Daisy surrounded her son with dignified women to reinforce his manners and teach him elegance. His childhood friends noticed that his casual, offhand manner and dapper dress gave him the bearing of a young nobleman,[[13]](#cite_note-Terkel-13) so they began calling him "Duke". Ellington credited his friend Edgar McEntee for the nickname: "I think he felt that in order for me to be eligible for his constant companionship, I should have a title. So he called me Duke."[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Though Ellington took piano lessons, he was more interested in [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball"). "President [[Theodore] Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") would come on his horse sometimes, and "stop and watch us play", he recalled.[[15]](#cite_note-15) Ellington went to [Armstrong Technical High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendship_Armstrong_Academy "Friendship Armstrong Academy") in Washington, D.C. His first job was selling peanuts at [Washington Senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Senators_(1901–1960) "Washington Senators (1901–1960)") baseball games.

**Alexander Calder** ([/ˈkɔːldər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); July 22, 1898 – November 11, 1976) was an American sculptor known both for his innovative [mobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_(sculpture) "Mobile (sculpture)") (kinetic sculptures powered by motors or air currents) that embrace chance in their aesthetic, his static "stabiles", and his monumental public sculptures.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Calder preferred not to analyze his work, saying, "Theories may be all very well for the artist himself, but they shouldn't be broadcast to other people."[[2]](#cite_note-2) His father, [Alexander Stirling Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Stirling_Calder "Alexander Stirling Calder"), and grandfather, [Alexander Milne Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Milne_Calder "Alexander Milne Calder"), were also sculptors.

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Calder&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Nanette-lederer-calder-and-alexander-calder-1900.jpg/250px-Nanette-lederer-calder-and-alexander-calder-1900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nanette-lederer-calder-and-alexander-calder-1900.jpg)

Nanette and Alexander Calder, photographed in 1900

Calder was born in 1898 in the Lawnton section of [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), Pennsylvania.[[3]](#cite_note-3) His birthdate remains a source of confusion. According to Calder's mother, Nanette (née Lederer), Calder was born on August 22, yet his birth certificate at Philadelphia City Hall, based on a hand-written ledger, stated July 22. When Calder's family learned of the birth certificate, they asserted with certainty that city officials had made a mistake. His mother was Jewish of [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bavaria "Kingdom of Bavaria") descent and his father was Calvinist of Scottish descent, but Calder never practiced a religion and rejected nationalism.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Calder's grandfather, sculptor [Alexander Milne Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Milne_Calder "Alexander Milne Calder"), was born in Scotland, had immigrated to Philadelphia in 1868, and is best known for the colossal statue of [William Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn "William Penn") on [Philadelphia City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_City_Hall "Philadelphia City Hall")'s tower. His father, [Alexander Stirling Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Stirling_Calder "Alexander Stirling Calder"), was a well-known sculptor who created many public installations, a majority of them in Philadelphia. Calder's mother was a professional portrait [artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting"), who had studied at the [Académie Julian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Académie_Julian "Académie Julian") and the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") in Paris from around 1888 until 1893. She moved to Philadelphia, where she met Stirling Calder while studying at the [Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Academy_of_the_Fine_Arts "Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts"). Calder's parents married on February 22, 1895. Alexander Calder's sister, Margaret Calder Hayes, was instrumental in the development of the [UC Berkeley Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley_Art_Museum "UC Berkeley Art Museum").[[6]](#cite_note-hayesthreecalders-6)

At the age of three, Calder posed nude for his father's sculpture *Man Cub*, a cast of which is in the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art") in New York City.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 12 In 1902 he also completed his earliest sculpture, a clay elephant.[[8]](#cite_note-8) In 1905 his father contracted [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis"), and Calder's parents moved to a ranch in [Oracle, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle,_Arizona "Oracle, Arizona"), leaving the children in the care of family friends for a year.[[9]](#cite_note-9) The children were reunited with their parents in March 1906 and stayed at the Arizona ranch during that summer.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 19[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The Calder family moved from Arizona to [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California"). The windowed cellar of the family home became Calder's first studio and he received his first set of tools. He used scraps of copper wire to make jewelry for his sister's dolls.[[11]](#cite_note-famsf.org-11) On January 1, 1907, Nanette Calder took her son to the [Tournament of Roses Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournament_of_Roses_Parade "Tournament of Roses Parade") in Pasadena, where he observed a four-horse-chariot race. This style of event later became the finale of Calder's miniature circus performances.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Calder would create two small sculptures around this time, depicting a dog and a duck, both fashioned from brass sheet metal.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 106-107 The dog was ostensibly made by Calder while the family was in Pasadena as a Christmas gift for his parents.[[6]](#cite_note-hayesthreecalders-6): 41 The small brass duck could be considered Calder's first mobile, as it featured a curved base that allowed it to rock when gently touched.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 108[[6]](#cite_note-hayesthreecalders-6): 41

In late 1909, the family returned to Philadelphia, where Calder briefly attended [Germantown Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germantown_Academy "Germantown Academy"), before the family settled in [Croton-on-Hudson, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croton-on-Hudson,_New_York "Croton-on-Hudson, New York") in 1910.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 117[[13]](#cite_note-13) During his high school years in Croton, Calder was befriended by his father's painter friend [Everett Shinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett_Shinn "Everett Shinn"), with whom he built a gravity-powered system of mechanical trains. Calder described it, "We ran the train on wooden rails held by spikes; a chunk of iron racing down the incline speeded the cars. We even lit up some cars with candle lights".[[14]](#cite_note-14) After Croton, the Calders moved to [Spuyten Duyvil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spuyten_Duyvil,_Bronx "Spuyten Duyvil, Bronx") in [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx") to be closer to New York City, as Stirling Calder was renting a studio in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village").[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 133 While living in Spuyten Duyvil, Calder attended high school in nearby [Yonkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonkers,_New_York "Yonkers, New York"). In 1912, Calder's father was appointed acting chief of the Department of Sculpture of the 1915 [Panama–Pacific International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama–Pacific_International_Exposition "Panama–Pacific International Exposition") in San Francisco, California,[[15]](#cite_note-15) and began work on sculptures for it.

During Calder's high school years of 1912–1915, the family moved back and forth between New York and California. In each new location, Calder's parents reserved cellar space as a studio for their son. Near the end of this period, Calder stayed with friends in California while his parents moved back to New York, so that he could graduate from [Lowell High School in San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_High_School_(San_Francisco) "Lowell High School (San Francisco)").[[16]](#cite_note-16) Calder graduated from high school in the class of 1915.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 151

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Calder&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Alexander Calder's parents did not want him to be an artist, so he decided to study mechanical engineering. An intuitive engineer since childhood, Calder did not even know what mechanical engineering was. "I was not very sure what this term meant, but I thought I'd better adopt it," he later wrote. He enrolled at the [Stevens Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens_Institute_of_Technology "Stevens Institute of Technology") in [Hoboken, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey "Hoboken, New Jersey"), in 1915.[[17]](#cite_note-HP-17) When asked why he decided to study mechanical engineering instead of art Calder said, "I wanted to be an engineer because some guy I rather liked was a mechanical engineer, that's all".[[18]](#cite_note-MW-18) At Stevens, Calder was a member of the [Delta Tau Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Tau_Delta "Delta Tau Delta") fraternity and excelled in mathematics.[[19]](#cite_note-19) He was well-liked and the class yearbook contained the following description, "Sand [Jump to content](#bodyContent)

**Alexander Calder** ([/ˈkɔːldər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); July 22, 1898 – November 11, 1976) was an American sculptor known both for his innovative [mobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_(sculpture) "Mobile (sculpture)") (kinetic sculptures powered by motors or air currents) that embrace chance in their aesthetic, his static "stabiles", and his monumental public sculptures.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Calder preferred not to analyze his work, saying, "Theories may be all very well for the artist himself, but they shouldn't be broadcast to other people."[[2]](#cite_note-2) His father, [Alexander Stirling Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Stirling_Calder "Alexander Stirling Calder"), and grandfather, [Alexander Milne Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Milne_Calder "Alexander Milne Calder"), were also sculptors.

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Calder&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Nanette-lederer-calder-and-alexander-calder-1900.jpg/250px-Nanette-lederer-calder-and-alexander-calder-1900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nanette-lederer-calder-and-alexander-calder-1900.jpg)

Nanette and Alexander Calder, photographed in 1900

Calder was born in 1898 in the Lawnton section of [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), Pennsylvania.[[3]](#cite_note-3) His birthdate remains a source of confusion. According to Calder's mother, Nanette (née Lederer), Calder was born on August 22, yet his birth certificate at Philadelphia City Hall, based on a hand-written ledger, stated July 22. When Calder's family learned of the birth certificate, they asserted with certainty that city officials had made a mistake. His mother was Jewish of [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bavaria "Kingdom of Bavaria") descent and his father was Calvinist of Scottish descent, but Calder never practiced a religion and rejected nationalism.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Calder's grandfather, sculptor [Alexander Milne Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Milne_Calder "Alexander Milne Calder"), was born in Scotland, had immigrated to Philadelphia in 1868, and is best known for the colossal statue of [William Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn "William Penn") on [Philadelphia City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_City_Hall "Philadelphia City Hall")'s tower. His father, [Alexander Stirling Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Stirling_Calder "Alexander Stirling Calder"), was a well-known sculptor who created many public installations, a majority of them in Philadelphia. Calder's mother was a professional portrait [artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting"), who had studied at the [Académie Julian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Académie_Julian "Académie Julian") and the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") in Paris from around 1888 until 1893. She moved to Philadelphia, where she met Stirling Calder while studying at the [Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Academy_of_the_Fine_Arts "Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts"). Calder's parents married on February 22, 1895. Alexander Calder's sister, Margaret Calder Hayes, was instrumental in the development of the [UC Berkeley Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley_Art_Museum "UC Berkeley Art Museum").[[6]](#cite_note-hayesthreecalders-6)

At the age of three, Calder posed nude for his father's sculpture *Man Cub*, a cast of which is in the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art") in New York City.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 12 In 1902 he also completed his earliest sculpture, a clay elephant.[[8]](#cite_note-8) In 1905 his father contracted [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis"), and Calder's parents moved to a ranch in [Oracle, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle,_Arizona "Oracle, Arizona"), leaving the children in the care of family friends for a year.[[9]](#cite_note-9) The children were reunited with their parents in March 1906 and stayed at the Arizona ranch during that summer.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 19[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The Calder family moved from Arizona to [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California"). The windowed cellar of the family home became Calder's first studio and he received his first set of tools. He used scraps of copper wire to make jewelry for his sister's dolls.[[11]](#cite_note-famsf.org-11) On January 1, 1907, Nanette Calder took her son to the [Tournament of Roses Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournament_of_Roses_Parade "Tournament of Roses Parade") in Pasadena, where he observed a four-horse-chariot race. This style of event later became the finale of Calder's miniature circus performances.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Calder would create two small sculptures around this time, depicting a dog and a duck, both fashioned from brass sheet metal.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 106-107 The dog was ostensibly made by Calder while the family was in Pasadena as a Christmas gift for his parents.[[6]](#cite_note-hayesthreecalders-6): 41 The small brass duck could be considered Calder's first mobile, as it featured a curved base that allowed it to rock when gently touched.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 108[[6]](#cite_note-hayesthreecalders-6): 41

In late 1909, the family returned to Philadelphia, where Calder briefly attended [Germantown Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germantown_Academy "Germantown Academy"), before the family settled in [Croton-on-Hudson, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croton-on-Hudson,_New_York "Croton-on-Hudson, New York") in 1910.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 117[[13]](#cite_note-13) During his high school years in Croton, Calder was befriended by his father's painter friend [Everett Shinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett_Shinn "Everett Shinn"), with whom he built a gravity-powered system of mechanical trains. Calder described it, "We ran the train on wooden rails held by spikes; a chunk of iron racing down the incline speeded the cars. We even lit up some cars with candle lights".[[14]](#cite_note-14) After Croton, the Calders moved to [Spuyten Duyvil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spuyten_Duyvil,_Bronx "Spuyten Duyvil, Bronx") in [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx") to be closer to New York City, as Stirling Calder was renting a studio in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village").[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 133 While living in Spuyten Duyvil, Calder attended high school in nearby [Yonkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonkers,_New_York "Yonkers, New York"). In 1912, Calder's father was appointed acting chief of the Department of Sculpture of the 1915 [Panama–Pacific International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama–Pacific_International_Exposition "Panama–Pacific International Exposition") in San Francisco, California,[[15]](#cite_note-15) and began work on sculptures for it.

During Calder's high school years of 1912–1915, the family moved back and forth between New York and California. In each new location, Calder's parents reserved cellar space as a studio for their son. Near the end of this period, Calder stayed with friends in California while his parents moved back to New York, so that he could graduate from [Lowell High School in San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_High_School_(San_Francisco) "Lowell High School (San Francisco)").[[16]](#cite_note-16) Calder graduated from high school in the class of 1915.[[7]](#cite_note-earlyyearsperl-7): 151

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Calder&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Alexander Calder's parents did not want him to be an artist, so he decided to study mechanical engineering. An intuitive engineer since childhood, Calder did not even know what mechanical engineering was. "I was not very sure what this term meant, but I thought I'd better adopt it," he later wrote. **John Ernst Steinbeck** ([/ˈstaɪnbɛk/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*STYNE-bek*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); February 27, 1902 – December 20, 1968) was an American writer and novelist. He won the [1962 Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1962 Nobel Prize in Literature") "for his realistic and imaginative writings, combining as they do sympathetic humor and keen social perception".[[2]](#cite_note-Literature1962-2) He has been called "a giant of American letters".[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Why_do_children_study_Of_Mice_and_Men?-4) One of the most widely read authors of the 20th century, he was also an independent journalist and war correspondent during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War").

During his writing career, he authored 33 books, with one book coauthored alongside [Edward Ricketts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Ricketts "Edward Ricketts"), including 16 novels, 6 [non-fiction books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction_book "Non-fiction book"), and 2 [collections of short stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collections_of_short_stories "Collections of short stories"). **Ellington** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") named after [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), an American composer, pianist, and leader of a jazz orchestra. It was named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2012.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Ellington is one of 110 [peak ring basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Within Ellington is the smaller crater [Berkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkel_(crater) "Berkel (crater)"). The somewhat smaller crater [Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derain_(crater) "Derain (crater)") is to the northwest. Both Derain and Ellington lie within a much older, 730-km-diameter, unnamed crater (referred to as b36).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The crater [Nasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_(crater) "Nasir (crater)") is to the south of Ellington.

# Disney (crater)

![}](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Disney-crater.png/330px-Disney-crater.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)
![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Disney_crater_labeled_by_NASA.png/250px-Disney_crater_labeled_by_NASA.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**Disney** is an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the H-15 (Bach) Quadrangle of [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)").[[1]](#cite_note-1) It was approved and adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") on Dec 19, 2012.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Disney is 113 km (70 mi) in diameter. This crater was named after [Walt Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney "Walt Disney") (Walter Elias), the American entrepreneur, voice actor, film producer, and animator. Disney is one of many craters named after notable art figures; per the [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), Mercury's craters are all named after a famous artist, composer, or writer who was influential for more than 50 years and deceased for more than three years at the time the crater was named.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Disney was named months after [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") acknowledged it for its resemblance to [Mickey Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mickey_Mouse "Mickey Mouse").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

# Calder (crater)

**Calder** is a small crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2013. Calder is named for the American sculptor [Alexander Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

[Villa-Lobos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa-Lobos_(crater) "Villa-Lobos (crater)") is to the northwest of Calder.

**Copland** is an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its floor is flooded with volcanic smooth plains material, which could be related to the activity that formed the nearby bright vent known as [Nathair Facula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathair_Facula "Nathair Facula").

## Naming

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Copland_(crater)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Naming")]

Amateur astronomer Ronald Dantowitz and his colleagues Scott Teare and Marek Kozubal used the Mt. Wilson 60-inch telescope in 1998 to observe a very bright feature on this portion of Mercury's surface, and they assumed that the bright feature was an impact crater. Mr. Dantowitz expressed his wish that the crater be named "Copland" (after American composer [Aaron Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Copland "Aaron Copland")) once better images of the area were obtained from spacecraft.

Surprisingly, *[MESSENGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESSENGER "MESSENGER")* images from Mercury flyby 3 revealed that the small bright feature, seen at the left edge of this image and now known as [Nathair Facula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathair_Facula "Nathair Facula"), is not an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") but more closely resembles a [volcanic vent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_vent "Volcanic vent"). No convention for naming volcanic vents on Mercury had yet been adopted, because none were identified prior to *MESSENGER*'s first Mercury flyby. A *MESSENGER* team member corresponded with Mr. Dantowitz and suggested that the name Copland be proposed instead for a large crater nearby. He agreed, and the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) approved the name Copland on March 3, 2010.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-IAU-2)

![}](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Cunningham_crater_EN1010038848M.jpg/330px-Cunningham_crater_EN1010038848M.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**Cunningham** is a young [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on the western floor of the [Caloris Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caloris_Basin "Caloris Basin"), on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It is surrounded by a bright [ray system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crater_ray "Crater ray").

The crater's name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2008, shortly after its discovery on the first flyby of [MESSENGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESSENGER "MESSENGER"). It is named for the American photographer [Imogen Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imogen_Cunningham "Imogen Cunningham").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

A confirmed *dark spot* is present in Cunningham crater.[[2]](#cite_note-2) This dark spot is associated with [hollows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury) "Hollows (Mercury)").

**Aaron Copland** ([/ˈkoʊplənd/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*KOHP-lənd*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) November 14, 1900 – December 2, 1990) was an American composer, critic, writer, teacher, pianist, and conductor of his own and other American music. Copland was referred to by his peers and critics as the "Dean of American Music". The open, slowly changing harmonies in much of his music are typical of what many consider the sound of American music, evoking the vast American landscape and pioneer spirit. He is best known for the works he wrote in the 1930s and 1940s in a deliberately accessible style often referred to as "populist" and which he called his "vernacular" style.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack1999186-3) Works in this vein include the ballets *[Appalachian Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Spring "Appalachian Spring")*, *[Billy the Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_the_Kid_(ballet) "Billy the Kid (ballet)")* and *[Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodeo_(ballet) "Rodeo (ballet)")*, his *[Fanfare for the Common Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanfare_for_the_Common_Man "Fanfare for the Common Man")* and [Third Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._3_(Copland) "Symphony No. 3 (Copland)"). In addition to his ballets and orchestral works, he produced music in many other genres, including chamber music, vocal works, opera, and film scores.

After some initial studies with composer [Rubin Goldmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_Goldmark "Rubin Goldmark"), Copland traveled to Paris, where he first studied with [Isidor Philipp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidor_Philipp "Isidor Philipp") and [Paul Vidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Vidal "Paul Vidal"), then with noted pedagogue [Nadia Boulanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadia_Boulanger "Nadia Boulanger"). He studied three years with Boulanger, whose eclectic approach to music inspired his own broad taste. Determined upon his return to the U.S. to make his way as a full-time composer, Copland gave lecture-recitals, wrote works on commission and did some teaching and writing. But he found that composing orchestral music in a [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism_(music) "Modernism (music)") style, which he had adopted while studying abroad, was unprofitable, particularly in light of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"). He shifted in the mid-1930s to a more accessible musical style that mirrored the German idea of *[Gebrauchsmusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gebrauchsmusik "Gebrauchsmusik")* ("music for use"), music that could serve utilitarian and artistic purposes. During the Depression years, he traveled extensively to Europe, Africa, and Mexico, formed an important friendship with Mexican composer [Carlos Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Chávez "Carlos Chávez"), and began composing his signature works.

During the late 1940s, Copland became aware that [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky") and other fellow composers had begun to study [Arnold Schoenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schoenberg "Arnold Schoenberg")'s use of [twelve-tone (serial) techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-tone_technique "Twelve-tone technique"). After he had been exposed to the works of French composer [Pierre Boulez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulez "Pierre Boulez"), he incorporated serial techniques into his *Piano Quartet* (1950), *Piano Fantasy* (1957), *[Connotations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connotations_(Copland) "Connotations (Copland)")* for orchestra (1961), and *[Inscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inscape_(Copland) "Inscape (Copland)")* for orchestra (1967). Unlike Schoenberg, Copland used his tone rows in much the same fashion as his tonal material—as sources for melodies and harmonies, rather than as complete statements in their own right, except for crucial events from a structural point of view. From the 1960s onward, Copland's activities turned more from composing to conducting. He became a frequent guest conductor of orchestras in the U.S. and the UK and made a series of recordings of his music, primarily for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records").

## Life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Copland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

### Early years

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Copland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Aaron Copland was born in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), New York, on November 14, 1900.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199915-4) He was the youngest of five children in a [Conservative Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Jewish "Conservative Jewish") immigrant family of [Lithuanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Jews "Lithuanian Jews") origin.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198419-5) While emigrating from Russia to the United States, Copland's father, Harris Morris Copland, lived and worked in Scotland for two to three years to pay for his boat fare to the United States. It was there that Copland's father may have [Anglicized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicized "Anglicized") his surname "Kaplan" to "Copland", though Copland himself believed for many years that the change had been caused by an [Ellis Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Island "Ellis Island") immigration official when his father entered the country.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199915-4)[[6]](#cite_note-Cone-6) Copland was unaware until late in his life that the family name had been Kaplan, his parents having never told him.[[6]](#cite_note-Cone-6) Throughout his childhood, Copland and his family lived above his parents' Brooklyn shop, H. M. Copland's, at 628 Washington Avenue (which Aaron later called "a kind of neighborhood [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's")"),[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199916-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) on the corner of Dean Street and Washington Avenue,[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoss2007266-9) and most of the children helped out in the store. His father was a staunch Democrat. The family members were active in [Congregation Baith Israel Anshei Emes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_Baith_Israel_Anshei_Emes "Congregation Baith Israel Anshei Emes"), where Aaron celebrated his [bar mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_mitzvah "Bar mitzvah"),[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199926-10) for which he studied under [Israel Goldfarb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Goldfarb "Israel Goldfarb").[[11]](#cite_note-jmrc-11) Not especially athletic, the sensitive young man became an avid reader and often read [Horatio Alger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Alger "Horatio Alger") stories on his front steps.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195315-12)

Copland's father had no musical interest. His mother, Sarah Mittenthal Copland, sang, played the piano, and arranged music lessons for her children.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199919-13) Copland had four older siblings: two brothers, Ralph and Leon, and two sisters, Laurine and Josephine.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Of his siblings, his oldest brother Ralph was the most advanced musically; he was proficient on the violin. Laurine had the strongest connection with Aaron; she gave him his first piano lessons, promoted his musical education, and supported him in his musical career.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199919-13) A student at the Metropolitan Opera School and frequent opera-goer, Laurine also brought home [libretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libretti "Libretti") for Aaron to study.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195317-16) Copland attended [Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boys_High_School_(Brooklyn) "Boys High School (Brooklyn)") and in the summer went to various camps. Most of his early exposure to music was at Jewish weddings and ceremonies, and occasional family musicales.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199926-10)

Copland began writing songs at the age of eight and a half.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17) His earliest notated music, about seven bars he wrote when age 11, was for an opera scenario he created and called *Zenatello*.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17)[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199932-18) From 1913 to 1917 he took piano lessons with Leopold Wolfsohn, who taught him the standard classical fare.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17) Copland's first public music performance was at a [Wanamaker's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanamaker's "Wanamaker's") recital.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195318-19)[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198423-20) By age 15, after attending a concert by Polish composer-pianist [Ignacy Jan Paderewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignacy_Jan_Paderewski "Ignacy Jan Paderewski"), Copland decided to become a composer.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199933-21) At 16, he heard his first symphony, at the [Brooklyn Academy of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Academy_of_Music "Brooklyn Academy of Music").[[22]](#cite_note-nyclgbtsites.org-22) After attempts to further his music study from a [correspondence course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correspondence_course "Correspondence course"), C
